source.filename: 2025-A continuum-based model for a layer jamming beam.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: The layer jamming structure can be modeled as a continuous medium under the assumption of infinitely many thin layers (layer thickness approaches zero while total beam height remains constant, delta/h << 1).
A plane stress state is assumed for material points following Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, with interlaminar normal strain neglected.

Elastic deformation-induced pressure between sheets is neglected, so maximum static friction per unit area is governed by Coulomb friction (mu * p, where p is vacuum pressure and mu is friction coefficient).
Material deformation behaves elastoplastically: purely elastic and reversible in the jamming state (|tau| < mu * p), and undergoing irreversible plastic sliding when yielding (|tau| >= mu * p).
Normal stress distribution is assumed continuous across the boundary separating jamming and sliding regions.
Shear stress in the sliding region is uniform (|tau| = mu * p), leading to the normal stress in the sliding region depending only on the beam longitudinal coordinate s.
The radius of curvature of the beam is significantly larger than the beam height.
Small deformations are assumed within each incremental loading step for large-deformation solutions.
control_variables: Beam dimensions in FEA (length = 40 mm, height = 5 mm, width/thickness = 20 mm)
Beam dimensions in physical experiment (length = 100 mm, height = 5 mm, width/thickness = 20 mm)
Finite element element type and mesh size (CPS4R elements with 0.1 mm edge length in Abaqus)
Confining pressure level during physical validation (60 kPa) and FEA (0.1 MPa)
Boundary condition: cantilever root fixed to a frame that slides along a rail to eliminate horizontal restraint
dependent_variables: Internal shear stress distribution tau(y, s)
Internal normal stress distribution sigma(y, s)
Vertical boundary between jamming and sliding regions (ys)
Critical shear force thresholds (Qslip and Qmax) separating full-jamming, half-slipping, and full-slipping states
Internal axial forces and bending moments (N, Q, M, NJ, MJ)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Treating a layer jamming structure as a continuum elastoplastic medium with continuous stress and strain fields across the height is valid for multi-layer beams (typically n >= 10).

The mechanical behavior of the layer jamming structure can be categorized into loading, yielding, and unloading stages, where yielding sliding corresponds to irreversible plastic deformation governed by Coulomb friction limits.

Analytical derivations determine specific threshold shear forces (Qslip = 2/3 * mu * p * b * h and Qmax) that define the boundaries between full jamming, half slipping, and full slipping cross-sectional states.
FEA simulations on 10-layer and 25-layer cantilevers demonstrate that stress distributions away from beam boundaries match continuum predictions and become smoother as layer count increases.
Neglecting interlaminar normal stress along the vertical axis in the analytical model causes an overestimation of the sliding region width compared to FEA.

Experimental load-deflection curves of a 20-layer PVC cantilever under 60 kPa vacuum pressure show that continuum model predictions fall entirely within the one standard deviation interval of measured data.

experimental_setup: Straight layer jamming cantilever specimen composed of 20 PVC sheets enclosed within a flexible PVC membrane (specimen dimensions: 100 mm length, 20 mm width/thickness, 5 mm height).
Specimen fixed to a mounting frame mounted on a free-sliding rail mechanism designed to release horizontal restraint.
Tensile testing machine used to apply transversal load and measure load-deflection behavior under a regulated vacuum pressure of 60 kPa.
future_work: Incorporation of boundary correction factors into the continuum model to better capture end effects near constraints and free ends.
Development of a more detailed analytical treatment of beam curvature in the jamming region under large-slip conditions.
Utilization of FEA for final verification of designs near free boundaries or under extreme loads causing full slipping.
independent_variables: Number of beam layers (10 and 25 in FEA; 20 in physical experiment)
Applied transverse load / concentrated force (e.g., 3 N, 4 N, 5.5 N in FEA; continuous loading in tensile testing)
Longitudinal position along the beam axis (s)
Vertical position across the beam cross-section height (y)
limitations_inferred: Experimental validation was restricted to a single material (PVC), static/quasi-static loading, and one pressure level (60 kPa), leaving performance under dynamic cyclic loading or varying pressure uncharacterized.
The continuum assumption cannot capture discrete layer phenomena such as individual sheet buckling or wrinkling when layer counts are small.
Interlayer friction is treated with an idealized constant Coulomb friction coefficient, omitting effects of surface wear, degradation, or pressure-dependent friction variation.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The model neglects interlaminar normal stress along the y-axis, which leads to an overestimation of the sliding region extent compared to FEA.
The continuum formulation does not explicitly account for constraint boundary or end effects, leading to discrepancies in shear stress distributions near cantilever ends (e.g., at s = 1 mm).

Significant shear stress discrepancies occur in the jamming region under the full-slipping state because the beam segments behave as curved beams, whereas the model assumes straight-beam shear stress patterns.
The model is less accurate under extreme loading leading to full slipping and near free boundaries.
main_results: The continuum-based layer jamming model (CLJM) successfully predicts internal shear stress, normal stress distributions, and deformation across full-jamming, half-slipping, and full-slipping states.
Closed-form critical shear force formulas were established: Qslip = (2/3) * mu * p * b * h for sliding initiation, and Qmax for transition to full slipping.
FEA simulations confirm that the continuum representation holds well for layer counts n >= 10, with stress distributions matching continuum predictions in central beam segments.
Experimental load-deflection measurements under 60 kPa confining pressure fall entirely within the analytical model's 1-sigma uncertainty band.
modeling_methods: Continuum mechanics modeling treating multi-layer systems as a continuous medium under the limit of infinite thin layers (delta -> 0, n -> infinity).
Euler-Bernoulli curved beam equilibrium formulations relating internal forces (axial force N, shear force Q, moment M) to distributed loads.
Sectional elastoplastic analysis in tau-sigma stress space implementing Coulomb friction slip criteria.
Step-by-step incremental algorithm to handle large external loads under small-deformation incremental steps.
Finite element analysis (FEA) using Abaqus with 2D plane-stress quadrilateral elements (CPS4R).
performance_metrics: Load-deflection response and deviation relative to the experimental mean and +/- 1 standard deviation interval
Agreement of predicted normal and shear stress profiles across the cross-section with FEA benchmarks
Extent and boundary position of the interlayer sliding zone (ys)
possible_gap_implications: Addressing boundary effects and curved-beam shear corrections analytically could enable accurate real-time control models for variable-stiffness soft robotic limbs and grippers without requiring computationally heavy FEA.

Extending the continuum formulation from 2D bending cantilevers to 3D spatial multi-axial deformations (torsion, tension, and out-of-plane bending) represents an important open research direction for continuum robots.
paper.research_objective: To develop a continuum-based analytical model (CLJM) that treats layer jamming structures with a large number of thin layers as a continuous medium to evaluate internal stress distributions (shear and normal stress) and deformation across full-jamming, half-slipping, and full-slipping states.
paper.research_problem: Existing analytical models for layer jamming structures typically model mechanics on a discrete layer-by-layer basis, making them impractical for multi-layer beams with numerous layers and failing to capture detailed continuous stress distributions and deformations with significant interlayer slip.
paper.title: A continuum-based model for a layer jamming beam
